specAnchors.text: describe the structures of an insect-pollinated and a wind-pollinated flower and explain how each is adapted for pollination

primer.text: Flowers cannot walk, so pollination depends on couriers. This note contrasts the two courier systems on the syllabus: flowers that hire insects with colour, scent and nectar, and flowers that let the wind do the deliveries. For each you will see how every structural detail, from petal size to filament length, earns its keep as an adaptation.

modules.title: Insect-Pollinated Flowers
modules.opening: An insect-visited flower runs a reward scheme: bold petals plus scent and nectar pull visitors in, and sticky pollen plus a sticky stigma make every visit count as a delivery between flowers.
keyPoints: Insect-pollinated flowers are large and brightly coloured so insects can spot them.
Scent and nectar reward visitors and push them to brush past the stamens.
Anthers sit on stiff filaments inside the flower so they rub pollen onto insect bodies.
Sticky stigmas positioned inside the flower catch pollen off arriving insects.

low.restatement: Colour, scent and nectar bring insects in; sticky pollen and sticky stigmas get the grains swapped between visits.
low.analogy: A shop with a bright window display and free samples: the customer leaves carrying crumbs to the next branch.
low.examPointer: Link every feature to its job — colour attracts, nectar rewards, stiff anthers load pollen, sticky stigmas unload it.

medium.restatement: The petals, scents and sugary rewards exist only to move pollen; the male parts are positioned where a feeding insect must brush them, and the female surface is tacky enough to strip grains off the visitor.
medium.analogy: A Velcro handshake: one side (the anther) coats the courier, the other (the stigma) grips the cargo on arrival.
medium.examPointer: Examiners want feature-to-function pairs, so name the structure and its adaptation in the same sentence.

modules.title: Wind-Pollinated Flowers
modules.opening: A wind-pollinated flower hires no couriers, so it drops every attractant and rebuilds its male and female surfaces as open platforms: long dangling anthers shed grains into moving air, and feathery stigmas sweep them back out of it.
keyPoints: Wind-pollinated petals stay small and dull, commonly green or brown.
No scent or nectar is made, because producing them would waste energy.
Anthers hang outside the flower on long filaments so wind can carry pollen away.
Feathery stigmas hang outside the flower to trap airborne grains.

low.restatement: No colour, no scent, no nectar; the anthers and stigmas simply hang outside where the air flows.
low.analogy: A stall that skips advertising and just throws flyers into the street wind, with a wide net to catch neighbours' flyers.
low.examPointer: The wind design is the inverse of the insect design — quote the hanging anthers and feathery stigmas as the pair of adaptations.

medium.restatement: Because random airflow is unreliable, the flower compensates with sheer exposure: anthers on long filaments launch grains beyond the petals, and feathery stigmas present a wide sticky net to whatever drifts past.
medium.analogy: Fishing without bait, using many hooks: wasteful per cast, effective across thousands of tries.
medium.examPointer: Say why the waste is acceptable: grains are cheap to make in bulk, so exposure beats attraction for these flowers.

glossary.definition: The transfer of pollen from a male flower part to a female flower part of the same species.
The male flower structure that makes and releases pollen grains.
The female flower surface that receives pollen grains.
The structure inside the ovary that holds the female gamete of a plant.
